annotations.text:
Direction D, executed modern — Plus Jakarta Sans, near-black ink on a cool off-white, one vivid teal, 22px cards on soft shadow.

Working controls, not pictures:
• Translator — the text ⇄ Morse toggle flips; tapping a letter chip selects it
• Speech — the mic cycles idle → listening → result, and the EN/PT switch changes the recognised copy
• Tap decode — press DURATION is measured for real. Tap for a dot, hold for a dash; 3 units of silence closes the letter, 7 closes the word. The cut-off stepper retunes it live.
• Settings — the threshold slider, speed and toggles all work
• Permission gates — the four states switch from the row at the bottom
• Translator · playing — the speaker button really plays: chips light letter by letter on ITU timing (dot 1, dash 3, gaps 1/3/7) and the speed chip retunes it live

App name is still open; "Morse" is a placeholder wordmark.
Settings, Learn and Tips scroll on a real phone. They are drawn here at full content height so the whole page can be reviewed at once — not as 844pt screens.

TABLET — 1180×820 landscape

One rule, two consequences:
• The bottom tab bar becomes a left rail. Same four destinations, same icons, settings drops to the bottom of the rail.
• Anything the phone stacks vertically splits into panes. Translator becomes input | output side by side; Learn puts the reading matter beside the reference grid, which reflows from 4 columns to 6.

Nothing here is a new screen — each is the phone layout above a width breakpoint, which is why it is worth settling now rather than retrofitting.

THREE UI LANGUAGES — English, Português (Brasil), Español

The whole interface translates, not just the input. These two are the same artboard as the English Translator with only the strings swapped, so any layout difference is purely string length.

What that surfaced: the Morse card's header row put its label and its hint on one line with no shrink protection. It fit in English at 390pt and would have collided at 360pt in Portuguese. Both now shrink and wrap; every phone frame was re-checked at 360pt.

Accented letters — decided: Ç (-.-..), É (..-..) and Ñ (--.--) have real ITU codes and are supported; every other diacritic is sent as its base letter. Ñ and Ç are distinct letters, not decoration (año ≠ ano), and the rest have no standard code. All three are in the Learn alphabet with the rule stated underneath.

OUTPUTS — one message, several channels

Decided 2026-09-03. There is ONE run of the message. The four cells choose which ways it goes out, and they are live: turn Light on mid-message and the torch joins the sound already in progress, in step. Turning them all off leaves Send it with nothing to do.

That replaces the old row, where Flash it was a separate primary action that merely switched the torch on and left it on. Flash it is now the Light channel; the primary button runs the message.

Why not one play button per output: pressing a second one mid-message would start that output from the beginning while the first is halfway through — the same message transmitted twice, out of step, with one progress bar unable to say which it was tracking.

Progress still reads twice: the chips carry played / sounding / pending, the thin track carries the exact position. Both describe the one run, whichever channels are carrying it.

Sound defaults ON, Light defaults OFF — decided 2026-09-03. Switching Light on is what raises the camera permission, and a new user's first press should not open a system dialog before they have heard anything. With every channel off the button is disabled rather than running a progress bar over silence. Screen and Vibrate are drawn but not built yet — they are in the strip now because retrofitting a fifth cell into a settled row is the expensive kind of change.

Still open: whether Vibrate can work on iOS at all. It cannot reproduce arbitrary durations there, which is why it was left until last.

FIRST RUN — three slides

Exists because Light starts off. Without it the torch is a feature nobody finds, and the strip looks like decoration.

The illustrations are the app's own components, not invented artwork: real letter chips, the real channel strip, the real Signal button. What the carousel promises is exactly what the next screen shows.

Slide 2 is the one that had to exist. It says plainly which channels are on, why Light is not, and that any of them can be changed at any time — including mid-message.

Skip jumps to the last slide rather than dismissing outright, so the Start button is always the way out. One way in, one way out.

Still open: whether this shows once ever, or again after an update that adds a channel. Screen and Vibrate are drawn in the strip but not built, so slide 2 will need revisiting when they land.
